blocks.text: A **Non-Performing Asset (NPA)** is a loan or advance on which the principal or interest has stayed overdue for **90 days**. An asset, including a leased asset, turns into an NPA when it stops generating income for the bank. Colloquially, NPAs are the bank's 'bad loans' or bad advances.

blocks.title: When does an account become an NPA?
rows: Interest and/or instalment of principal overdue for **more than 90 days**
The bill remains overdue for **more than 90 days**
An instalment of principal or interest overdue for **two crop seasons**
An instalment of principal or interest overdue for **one crop season**

blocks.title: Quarter rule
blocks.text: A bank should classify an account as an NPA only if the interest charged during a quarter is **not fully serviced within 90 days from the end of that quarter**. Ninety days is the magic number.

blocks.title: Crop seasons
blocks.phrase: Short crop, two seasons of wait; long crop, just one.
letters: Short
Short-duration crops: NPA after **two** crop seasons overdue
Long
Long-duration crops: NPA after **one** crop season overdue
blocks.note: The longer the crop takes to grow, the less patience the rule allows: opposite of what you might guess.

blocks.title: Two key terms
rows: Any amount due to the bank under a credit facility that is **not paid on the due date** fixed by the bank.
An OD/CC account is out of order if the outstanding balance stays **continuously above the sanctioned limit or drawing power**.

blocks.title: Another way an account is 'out of order'
items: The outstanding balance is **below** the sanctioned limit or drawing power, but there are **no credits continuously for ninety days** as on the date of the balance sheet.
Or the credits during that period are **not enough to cover the interest** debited in the same period.

blocks.title: Link to NPA
blocks.text: 'Out of order' is the NPA trigger for **overdraft and cash credit** accounts, just as '90 days overdue' is the trigger for term loans and bills.

A Presidential Ordinance (promulgated in 2017, amending the Banking Regulation Act, 1949) strengthened the RBI's hand against bad loans. It empowered the RBI to enforce **expeditious resolution** of banks' NPAs and boosted the central bank's legal empowerment to crack down on them.

blocks.title: Key features and effects
items: The Union Government empowered itself to direct the RBI to start the NPA resolution process once a default is established.
It lets the political establishment act as a proactive agent in bank NPA resolution.
It carries a political risk: the Government may be accused of picking and choosing which default cases go for resolution.
The provisions of the **Bankruptcy Code** were linked to the **Banking Regulation Act**.
It allows the RBI to set up **oversight committees** for banks with NPAs.
It was expected to affect the economy, banks' lending behaviour and the investment climate.

blocks.title: Who allowed oversight committees?
blocks.text: The power to set up oversight committees for banks with NPAs came from the **Presidential Ordinance**, not from the original RBI Act, 1934 or the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 as such.
Banks sort NPAs into **three categories** based on how long the asset has been non-performing and how realisable the dues are. The rules below apply with effect from **31 March 2005**.

blocks.title: Three NPA categories
rows: Has remained an NPA for **12 months or less**
Has remained in the substandard category for **12 months**
Loss identified by the bank's internal or external auditors or the RBI inspection, but **not yet written off wholly**; considered uncollectible, though some salvage value may remain

blocks.title: Slide of an asset after default
items: Standard (performing)
Earns income normally
Substandard NPA
NPA for 12 months or less
Doubtful NPA
12 months in substandard
Loss asset
Uncollectible; should be written off

blocks.title: Order of NPA categories
blocks.phrase: SDL: Slowly Deteriorating Loan - Substandard, then Doubtful, then Loss.
letters: S
Substandard: NPA up to 12 months
D
Doubtful: 12 months as substandard
L
Loss: uncollectible, to be written off
blocks.note: Tangible assets and standard assets are NOT NPA categories; standard assets are performing.

blocks.text: **Provisioning** means setting aside part of profits to cover possible loan losses. The rates below are as given in the 2024-25 book and the RBI revises them from time to time, so use them as the exam reference but check for later circulars.

blocks.title: Provisioning by asset type (as per the book)
rows: Write off; if kept on books, provide **100 per cent** of the outstanding
**100 per cent** of the extent not covered by the realisable value of security
From **20 per cent to 100 per cent** of the secured portion, depending on how long it has been doubtful
General provision of **10 per cent** of total outstanding, with no allowance for ECGC cover or security
Additional 10 per cent, so a total of **20 per cent**

blocks.title: Standard asset provisions (general provisions on funded outstanding)
rows: **1 per cent** for personal loans, capital-market exposures, residential housing loans beyond Rs 20 lakh and commercial real estate loans
Additional facilities under a BIFR or term-lender package
No provision needed for **one year** from the date of disbursement

blocks.title: Unsecured exposure and security
rows: Exposure where the realisable value of the security is **not more than 10 per cent** ab initio of the outstanding exposure.
Includes all funded and non-funded exposures (including underwriting and similar commitments).
Only **tangible** security properly discharged to the bank; guarantees, comfort letters and similar items do not count.

blocks.title: Standard asset rates
blocks.phrase: Farmers pay a quarter, risky-personal-property pays one, the rest pay forty paise.
letters: Agriculture and SME (a quarter of a per cent)
Personal loans, capital-market exposures, large housing (beyond Rs 20 lakh), commercial real estate
All other advances

blocks.title: Where 100 appears
blocks.phrase: When the money is gone or unsecured and doubtful, provide a full hundred.
letters: Loss
100 per cent if kept on the books
Doubtful
100 per cent on the unsecured part
blocks.note: Substandard is the mild one: 10 per cent, or 20 per cent if unsecured.

blocks.text: The **Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest (SARFAESI) Act, 2002** was enacted to regulate securitisation and reconstruction of financial assets and to enforce security interests created over them, so that such assets can be realised. It was passed on **17 December 2002**.

blocks.title: Why it matters
items: A secured creditor can enforce its security interest **without the intervention of a court or tribunal**.
Before the Act, lenders had to file **civil suits** in courts, a long and time-consuming route.
Banks and financial institutions can directly **auction pledged residential or commercial property** to recover loans.

blocks.title: Recovery under SARFAESI
items: The borrower defaults on a loan that is backed by collateral.
The secured creditor serves a **notice**; the borrower gets **60 days (2 months)** to repay.
If the borrower still does not pay, the lender can **take possession** of the pledged assets.
The lender can take over management of the assets, appoint a person to manage them, or ask the borrower's debtors to pay their dues for that asset.

An aggrieved borrower can approach the **Debts Recovery Tribunal (DRT)**; to appeal against the DRT decision before the **DRAT** (Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunal) the borrower must deposit **50 per cent** of the amount.

blocks.title: SARFAESI numbers
blocks.phrase: 2002 Act, 17 December; 60 days notice; 50 per cent deposit to appeal at DRAT.
letters: Year of the SARFAESI Act (passed 17 December)
Days of notice (two months) to the borrower
Deposit needed for an appeal to the DRAT

blocks.title: Tribunal ladder
blocks.text: SARFAESI recovery itself avoids courts. Appeals go first to the **DRT**, then to the **DRAT** (with the 50 per cent deposit).

blocks.title: Drawbacks and answers
items: A major drawback: the Act does **not apply to unsecured creditors**.
This and other gaps in the recovery mechanism were plugged by the **Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016**.
**Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs)** buy out distressed assets, giving banks another way to offload doubtful debt for more focused and efficient resolution.

blocks.title: Three recovery routes
rows: Enforcement of security by secured creditors without going to court.
Covers gaps in recovery, including cases involving unsecured creditors.
Buy distressed assets from banks so that banks can clean up their books.

blocks.title: Secured only
blocks.text: SARFAESI works only where the loan is **secured by collateral**. Unsecured creditors cannot use it, which is why the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 was needed.

blocks.title: Co-operative banks join SARFAESI
items: Co-operative banks are initially not covered by the definition of banks eligible for SARFAESI.
A **notification** (without amending the law) brings co-operative banks into the class of banks entitled to use SARFAESI.
The Government **amends the Act** to include co-operative banks formally in the definition of banks.
The **Supreme Court** rules in favour of co-operative banks invoking SARFAESI, settling petitions that questioned the notification and Parliament's power to amend.

blocks.title: Why it is important
items: The Indian banking system has **more than 1,500 urban co-operative banks (UCBs)** and about **1 lakh rural co-operative banks**, with large retail deposits (as per the book).
Speedy recovery of bad loans is vital for their smooth functioning; SARFAESI avoids long delays in civil courts and co-operative tribunals.
The RBI has placed lending and deposit-taking restrictions on several co-operative banks, with **PMC Bank** and **CKP Bank** cited as cases.

When a co-operative bank comes under RBI restrictions, depositors' money is often stuck for years; easier recovery through SARFAESI can speed up liquidation or resolution and supports the safety of deposits.

blocks.title: Three dates for co-op banks
blocks.phrase: 03 notified, 13 amended, 20 settled: notification, Act change, then the Supreme Court.
letters: Notification brings co-operative banks under SARFAESI
Act amended to include co-operative banks formally
Supreme Court upholds it on 5 May

revision: An NPA is a loan whose principal or interest remains overdue for 90 days.
NPA tests: term loan over 90 days; OD/CC out of order; bills over 90 days; crops: two seasons (short) or one season (long).
Classify as NPA only if interest charged in a quarter is not fully serviced within 90 days of quarter-end.
Out of order: balance continuously above limit or drawing power, or no credits for 90 days or credits less than interest.
Three NPA categories: substandard, doubtful and loss. Standard assets are not NPAs.
Substandard: NPA up to 12 months. Doubtful: 12 months as substandard. Loss: uncollectible, not yet written off.
Provisioning per the book: substandard 10 per cent (20 per cent if unsecured); unsecured doubtful and loss assets 100 per cent.
Standard asset provisions: 0.25 per cent for agriculture and SME, 1 per cent for specified sectors, 0.40 per cent for others.
The Presidential Ordinance empowered the RBI to push NPA resolution and set up oversight committees; Bankruptcy Code linked to the Banking Regulation Act.
SARFAESI Act 2002 (passed 17 Dec 2002) lets secured creditors recover dues without courts or tribunals.
SARFAESI: 60-day notice, then possession and management of pledged assets.
Appeal to DRAT against a DRT decision requires a deposit of 50 per cent of the amount.
SARFAESI does not cover unsecured creditors; gaps were plugged by the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016.
ARCs buy distressed assets from banks to clean their books.
Co-operative banks: notified 2003, Act amended 2013, Supreme Court ruling 5 May 2020.
